cells.tense: You are here with the pen, seeing the shape and not just the parts.
cells.ask: Pick one thing you understand well and describe how it works out loud to someone, plainly, without dressing it up. Then stop and let it stand.
cells.core:
You can see how something works underneath how it looks. Not a theory you carry around — it's right there when you look, and you trust it enough to use it. That's rare, and most days you spend it without noticing.

The quiet risk is feeding it more pattern when what it wants is to rest in what you already see. So let one of these patterns go untested. Say the shape out loud to someone, in plain words. It doesn't need to be finished or defended. When you do, you find out which patterns hold up once they leave your head — and the ones that hold are the ones worth keeping.

cells.tense: You are bracing for a depth that isn't here yet.
cells.ask: Pick one pattern you've been working and say its structure out loud to someone who doesn't share your background. If it lands, leave it. If not, name what's missing.
cells.core:
You're pushing the pattern further than it needs to go. Somewhere ahead is the version where all the pieces finally lock, and you're living there — so a talk becomes a test of whether it's complete. The depth you're reaching for is eating what the depth was for.

A pattern isn't proven by how far you take it alone. Put one of these structures in front of somebody else, in words they can answer. Not to be told you're right — to find out whether it still makes sense once it leaves your head. What comes back shows you where the structure is solid and where you're the one holding it up.
cells.sheetLine: Depth isn't proof. Say it where someone can answer.

cells.tense: You are standing at a door that is already behind you.
cells.ask: Send one thing you see — a pattern, a way something works — to someone who'd use it. Just the plain version, no fixing required.
cells.core:
Seeing how a thing is put together is one of the ways you're most yourself. When it's working well you don't hoard the shape — you hand it to whoever it belongs to and let them walk with it. No need to check that they got it right. The pattern leaves your head and gets used, and that's the whole exchange.

Lately that handoff has gone quiet. You still see, and you don't say. What's empty is the handing over, not the eye. So put one pattern where someone else can pick it up: tell them how something works, in words they can use, and let that be the whole job. No follow-up, no defending it. The rest can stay where it is for now.

cells.tense: You are already reading the pattern while saying the pattern is reading you.
cells.ask: Name one pattern you've been treating as just how things go, and say out loud that you're the one who spotted it. No explaining — just the claim.
cells.core:
You read patterns faster than anyone in the room, and when you talk about it the shape just seems to emerge. As if the thing did the spotting instead of you. But you're the one who caught it. That's what you're working with — sharp sight that keeps getting filed under how things are.

Say it once, out loud, to nobody in particular. Not the mechanism — just that you're the one who saw it. It doesn't need to be proven or explained, and nobody has to agree. One sentence where you take the credit that's already yours by default. Everything after that can stay exactly as it is.
cells.sheetLine: You already read it. The claim is still yours to make.
